mp.note:
Like I said in my email, would also speak in meetings of afdeelingen. 
Also, the way a Kamerlid and a Minister speak in Parliament is quite similar. Both speak only when recognized and both address the Chair.

clerk.note: Split this type: Griffier is not a stenographer. Stenographers write the minutes, griffier is in charge of the administrative side of the Kamer, but is not a stenographer. I don't know if you want to keep the role of Griffier, but it is definitely not the same as stenographer.

spk-T_._Mackay_.note:
Note that this man has an initial, rather than just a last name. This is because he was an MP at the same time as another man named Mackay, so they used their initials to distinguish the two.

He was member of the Anti-Revolutionalre Partij initially, and transferred to the Vrij-Antirevolutionaire Partij in 1896. I'm not sure which he was on this specific date, but he was not partyless.

pair-036.ref: "MP" as an abbreviation of Member of Parliament is not a term that is used in Dutch. They would be more likely to describe themselves as "Kamerlid". Furthermore, in 1899-1900, "Staten-Generaal" is needelessly unspecific. Someone would either be a member of the Eerste Kamer (Senate) or the Tweede Kamer (House of Representatives). So a more plausible answer would be "Kamerlid in de Eerste/Tweede Kamer"

pair-003.ref: Ik ben zelf de Voorzitter, dus hier kan geen sprake van zijn.

stenographer.note: The stenographer records recognised floor speech and the Chair’s rulings. Asides and unrecognised interruptions are only recorded if the recognized speaker responds to them.

proc-009.note: It is unlikely that a speech would start with saying "Mijnheer de Voorzitter!" twice. I notice that it does appear twice in most of these excerpts. It would be more likely to have it once.

proc-004.note:
This is not someone's speech: this is the Handelingen describing what is happening (someone presents a report, and the decision is made to print and distribute the report is made, none of this is part of a speech). So: yes ,the Chair would have allowed this, the stenographer would have recorded it and there's no anachronism, but "speaks after recognition" is not an accurate description for what is happening here.

Also, various OCR mistakes. "éê" --> "één" "he t Verslag in d e" --> "het Verslag in de" and more
